item.title: Nvidia crisis: Senate panel summons Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick to testify
item.description: Senior US officials are discussing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's possible exit as lawmakers question the administration's oversight of advanced AI chip exports to China ...
item.dc:creator: Agencies
item.content:encoded: Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee as Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy raises national security concerns. Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina, on Thursday evening sent letters to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive United States (US) technology,” Scott said in a social media post, adding, “The American people deserve answers.”  Congressional leaders of both political parties have said they support efforts to hear from Huang directly about his entanglement with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who US officials concluded had been recruited by China’s main spy agency. Scott asked Huang to appear on December 3 by his own volition but also threatened that the committee could issue a subpoena. House Republicans also said on Thursday they were in discussions with Huang to testify before other committees. Huang has hired lawyers who previously represented executives in government investigations, according to people familiar with the matter. Senior White House officials are discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out amid a spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s now-former CEO Jensen Huang, two people familiar with the situation said on Thursday. A growing number of lawmakers criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China. Criticism of Lutnick’s actions predates Thursday’s resignation of Huang, who said he would step down as chief executive officer (CEO) of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. But the charge that Lutnick has not done enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China has emerged as the fallout from Jensen Huang’s actions grows. Earlier on Thursday, a White House official said President Donald Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position.” In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held off adding China’s AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and over 100 other firms flagged as national security risks to a trade blacklist. Asked on CNN if Lutnick should lose his job, Republican Senator John Kennedy said: “I don’t know yet.” He and others have urged Lutnick to quickly publicly answer questions and noted he will be called to appear before Congress. “This is as serious as an aneurism.” The US has not posted any additions to that list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in over a decade. Reuters earlier reported that the US Commerce Department has not added new Chinese companies to that list for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee starting in January, and incoming Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chair Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat, wrote to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, telling the administration to preserve all documents related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced AI chips to China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday his department had favored putting Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed on the US entity list for months but it was up to the Commerce Department to act, adding that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) could possibly take other action. He added that the administration was working to shut down “leakage” in the chip export system.

Home / World News / Trump, Xi, Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on sidelines of APEC

Trump, Xi, Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on sidelines of APEC While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs

A worker pushes a row of trolleys past a promotion board for the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport, in Shenzhen, China | Image: Reuters

AP Washington 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 7:53 AM IST

Listen to This Article

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen, an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers. While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs, and they will be heavier in symbolism than substance. Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed on Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.

Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the US war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers. Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly five-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran. Also Read

Nvidia crisis: Senate panel summons Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick to testify

US midterms deepen uncertainty over future policy and ties with India premium

US midterm upset leaves India facing a tougher regional recalibration premium

Five things to know about APEC as Trump, Putin and Xi set to attend summit

The US president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the US war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty -- known as New START -- expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for "a new, improved and modernised" deal that includes China. But Beijing's arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the US and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With US and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.

Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige. "I would be shocked if there were a joint statement that came out of this meeting that said anything about denuclearisation," said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing. "I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signalling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they're making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don't like," Kagan said.

The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades. More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia's war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.

The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University. "You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism," he said. The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years Putin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as "dear friend."   Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.

Beijing is the Number one trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022. As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia's energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies. In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a "no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv's Western allies played a part in provoking Russia's military action in Ukraine.

Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing's policy on issues related to Taiwan. Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back. Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalised plans for establishing the United Nations.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others. "It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.

item.title: Microsoft outage eases after over a day, recovery timeline uncertain
item.description: Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant and that a broader rollout of software fixes was stabilizing the system ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Microsoft outage eases after over a day, recovery timeline uncertain

Microsoft outage eases after over a day, recovery timeline uncertain Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant and that a broader rollout of software fixes was stabilizing the system

Microsoft services, including Teams, Outlook, Copilot and several Microsoft 365 applications, affecting users worldwide on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.(Photo:PTI)

Reuters 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 7:38 AM IST

Listen to This Article

A global outage of Microsoft Outlook and Teams was easing on Friday after more than 24 hours of disruption crippled online communications across businesses and governments, though the company said it still had no timeline for full recovery of services. Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant and that a broader rollout of software fixes was stabilizing the system. It said it was not aware of any malicious activity and ruled out AI as the cause. Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.

It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements. Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared. Also Read

Global Microsoft outage disrupts India's corporate workday rhythm

Microsoft disruption exposes risks of relying on single provider: Experts

Microsoft service disruption impacts IndiGo's email support services

Microsoft 365 outage continues as company sees limited recovery in services

Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook, Teams for hours, hits users globally

ANOTHER OUTAGE FOR MICROSOFT The outage, reports of which started climbing around 1725 GMT on Thursday according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year. Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online - its cloud-based email and scheduling hub - leaving unconnected applications operational.

The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft's workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector's parent company, Ookla. Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels. "It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider's email and collaboration tools," said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla. Microsoft shares closed flat at $523.88 on Friday. The stock has gained roughly 8% so far this year.

Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS. De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between $300 million and $500 million, well below the $400 million to $1.5 billion financial toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than 8 million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions. Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.

"The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year," said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro. "If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider's hands." Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations. TRADES HAD TO BE CONFIRMED BY FAX A spokesperson for the UK government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organizations such as the NHS and London's Metropolitan Police.

Lack of access to emails and other services was impacting the Metropolitan Police's ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected. The NHS said its local services were turning to alternate measures such as using IT systems or paper records. For businesses, the fallout was widespread. European exchange operator Euronext reported email disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates. American AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft connectors, while Indian airlines IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India said their email support services were impacted.

The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers, and investment trust companies. One of the companies went as far as cancelling a bond repurchase transaction, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters. Another Taiwanese financial company resorted to using fax to confirm trades, a second source said. In the US, electric truck maker Workhorse Group rescheduled its results on Thursday to November 16, while Switzerland's Richemont briefly delayed its first-half results announcement on Friday. In Australia, where the spy agency and federal police were among organizations caught in the outage, Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft does not suspect a cyberattack.

"The impact that they are dealing with ... is very much on email systems," the minister added.

item.title: US lawmakers push for tougher curbs on advanced AI chip exports to China
item.description: US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Huang ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US lawmakers push for tougher curbs on advanced AI chip exports to China

US lawmakers push for tougher curbs on advanced AI chip exports to China US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Huang

The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China | Image: Bloomberg

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 1:30 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Chinese AI shares tumbled on Friday, as investors worried that Jensen Huang's departure as Nvidia CEO could further restrict Chinese access to advanced US chips, deepening the technology divide between the world's two biggest economies.   US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Huang, who has pushed to preserve access to the Chinese market and has close ties with US President Donald Trump.   Huang stepped down after news reports of a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.

Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China's surging AI development.   Senior White House officials were also discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation said, as the desire to take action rose across Washington. Also Read

Alice Huang had stake in China data centre serving Huawei, says report

From gaming chips to AI dominance: How Nvidia became a tech powerhouse

Fallout from Nvidia scandal may dampen investor exuberance around AI boom

US lawmakers step up pressure on Howard Lutnick as Nvidia row deepens

Meet Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim CEO after Jensen Huang's exit

A growing number of lawmakers have criticized Lutnick for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a US trade blacklist, and questioned whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China.   Nvidia's advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China's access to Nvidia's chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

"The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here," Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favored limiting China's access to the advanced technology. "I think there's a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take."   Investors dumped shares in Chinese AI models and hardware suppliers to the US on Friday, with AI model stocks Z.AI and MiniMax Group tumbling 12% and 8.4% respectively.   Data center suppliers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology, whose businesses are heavily reliant on US markets, also slumped more than 8%.   The Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.

REPUBLICANS EYE EXPORT RESTRICTIONS   The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.   Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company's chips remotely.   Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense  authorization bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.   The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers to access Nvidia chips.  SCRUTINY OF HUANG LIKELY TO CONTINUE   Huang's resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation.

"Congress can still subpoena him and Nvidia should conduct an independent investigation to determine whether the problems extend beyond Huang," Cheung said.   Cheung said Huang's departure could weaken Nvidia's influence in Washington and create additional momentum for legislation that tightens restrictions on advanced chip exports. He said Nvidia's new leadership could also reconsider the company's China strategy as it seeks to rebuild trust with US policymakers.   Jensen Huang is separately expected to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke with Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for his testimony.

Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with Alice Huang.
